I asked 8 Scrum Masters to define cycle time. I got 8 different answers.

At ABB, when I first started tracking flow metrics, I assumed cycle time and lead time were the same thing. A lot of people do.

They are not — and confusing them will send you after the wrong problem.

Lead time is the full clock: from the moment a stakeholder makes a request, to the moment it is delivered. This is the experience from the outside.

Cycle time is the active work clock: from when a developer picks up a ticket, to when it is done. This is the experience from the inside.

When I mapped both for our team at ABB, I found something striking: our cycle time was 2.3 days. Our lead time was 11 days. The actual work was fast. The waiting was the problem.

Stories sat in the backlog for over a week before anyone touched them. Once started, they moved quickly. The bottleneck was not the team — it was the intake process and prioritisation.

If I had only looked at cycle time, I would have optimised the wrong thing. Lead time showed me where the real waste was hiding.

One chart changed how my entire team talked about delivery.

At Adidas, we had 78 items in progress at any given time. Twelve were blocked. Lead time was averaging 11.6 days. Everyone could feel the slowdown — but nobody could explain where it was coming from.

I introduced a Cumulative Flow Diagram to the team. Most of them had never seen one before.

A CFD tracks how many items are in each stage of your workflow over time. When everything is flowing well, the bands stay roughly parallel and consistent in width. When a stage becomes a bottleneck, its band widens — work piles up and stops moving.

Our CFD made the problem immediately visible. The testing band had grown by 35% over the previous two weeks. Development was completing work and pushing it into testing faster than testing could absorb it. The widening band was the bottleneck — not the team's effort, not unclear requirements.

When one band widens, flow slows. That is the insight the CFD gives you that no status report ever could.

We used the data to make a concrete decision: two developers temporarily shifted to support testing until the queue cleared. Within one sprint, the testing band stabilised. Cycle time dropped from 5.2 days to 3.8 days.

A CFD does not just show you what happened. It shows you where to look next.

Security issues: 23 open, with 6 high severity.

The biggest debt driver was Order Service at 26% — a core component touched by almost every sprint. Cyclomatic complexity was at 14.2, just below the 15 threshold where code becomes genuinely hard to change safely.

Nobody had hidden this. It simply had never been measured or made visible.

I created a technical debt dashboard and started reviewing it in every sprint retrospective — not to blame, but to make informed trade-off decisions. How much debt do we pay down this sprint versus how much new feature work do we take on?

Code quality improved from 84 to 92 within four sprints. Code coverage moved from 80% toward the 90% target. Delivery speed actually increased because developers stopped navigating around landmines they now understood.

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Technical debt is no different.
